title: The entry point of Fermat's two-squares descent
statement: Let p > 0 with 1 + 1 <= p, and let x satisfy x*x = -1 (mod p). Then there are k and c with k*p = c*c + 1*1 and 0 < k < p. That is: a multiple of p is a sum of two squares, and the multiplier is ALREADY strictly between 0 and p -- which is the invariant the descent's induction needs, and the reason the representative has to be centered before the divisibility is read off. Primality is deliberately NOT a hypothesis: everything here needs only 0 < p and 1 + 1 <= p, and the caller derives the second from p = 2m+1 with m even and p prime, which is Nat work that does not belong in an Int order module.

formal.statement: theorem Int.exists_small_multiple_of_sq_add_one : ((x0 : Int) -> ((x1 : Int) -> ((x2 : Int.lt Int.zero x0) -> ((x3 : Int.le (Int.add Int.one Int.one) x0) -> ((x4 : Int.ModEq x0 (Int.mul x1 x1) (Int.neg Int.one)) -> Exists.{1} Int (fun (x5 : Int) => Exists.{1} Int (fun (x6 : Int) => And (Eq.{1} Int (Int.mul x5 x0) (Int.add (Int.mul x6 x6) (Int.mul Int.one Int.one))) (And (Int.lt Int.zero x5) (Int.lt x5 x0)))))))))

provenance.source: the entry step of Euler's descent proof (1749) of Fermat's two-square theorem: from -1 being a quadratic residue mod p, some multiple of p below p^2 is a sum of two squares

notes: This is the declaration `two_squares.rs`'s module doc claims already landed under the name `declare_exists_mul_isSumOfTwoSquares_of_residue`. IT DID NOT: measured 2026-09-05, that name occurs exactly once in the file, inside the doc comment, and is not in `declare_two_squares_all`. This row is the first time the entry point exists. The route is five steps, all from lemmas already in the environment: center x modulo p (F:int-exists-centered-representative), square the congruence (Int.ModEq.mul) so c*c = -1, read off p | c*c - (-1) = c*c + 1*1 (Int.ModEq.dvd) giving k with c*c + 1*1 = p*k, get 0 < k from c*c + 1*1 being positive, and k < p from F:int-sq-add-sq-lt-sq-of-bounds at e := 1 putting c*c + 1*1 strictly under p*p. Centering FIRST is what makes the last step available; the uncentered x has no bound at all, and that is exactly why the previous slice could not close this. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it is not Fermat's theorem. F:int-fermat-two-squares remains open, and its notes size the three pieces still missing -- the divisibility m | c*c + e*e that produces the NEXT multiplier, the q != 0 argument (the only step that consumes primality), and the Nat.strongInduction assembly.
